cards.front: An interviewer asks: ‘What’s the time complexity of your solution?’ What does a strong answer include?
cards.back: The Big-O bound, which case it describes (best/average/worst), the dominant operation driving it, and the space complexity — said out loud while pointing at the code, e.g. ‘O(n log n) time worst case from the sort, O(n) space for the output.’

cards.front: Time vs space: how do you discuss the tradeoff?
cards.back: As the two axes every solution is measured on: faster often costs memory (hash maps, memoization, caches), leaner often costs time (recompute vs store). The interview line: ‘I’ll name both complexities for every solution I propose.’

cards.front: How do you explain amortized analysis of a dynamic array in an interview?
cards.back: ‘Appending is O(1) amortized: most appends are constant time, and the occasional doubling resize costs O(n) but happens rarely enough that the cost spreads to O(1) per append across a sequence of n appends.’

cards.front: Why do interviewers ask for best, average, AND worst case?
cards.back: Because the bound alone hides behavior: quicksort is O(n log n) average but O(n²) worst case on sorted input — and the input distribution in the real system decides which one you actually pay.

cards.front: How do you derive log n and n log n on the spot?
cards.back: ‘Halving the problem each step gives log n levels — binary search. Divide-and-conquer that does linear work per level, like mergesort, gives n work × log n levels = n log n.’ Say the recurrence, then the level count.

quiz.q: Stating complexity aloud during coding:
choices: Makes your reasoning gradable and forces self-checks
quiz.explain: Verbalized reasoning is scorable reasoning — and it catches your own mistakes mid-stream.

quiz.q: Binary search on n sorted elements is O(log n) because:
choices: Each comparison halves the remaining search space
quiz.explain: Halving n times reaches 1 element: the number of halvings is log₂ n.

quiz.q: Quicksort with a naive first-element pivot on an already-sorted array degrades to:
quiz.explain: Bad pivots make partitions maximally unbalanced: n levels of n work each.

quiz.q: A dynamic array doubles its capacity when full. The amortized cost per append is:
quiz.explain: The O(n) copy cost of a resize is spread over the ~n/2 appends since the last resize: O(1) each.

cards.front: When do you reach for two pointers?
cards.back: Ordered data and pair-finding: opposite ends for sorted two-sum or container-with-most-water; same-direction fast/slow pointers for cycle detection or in-place dedup — O(n) time, O(1) space. Name which variant and why.

cards.front: Sliding window vs two pointers: what’s the distinction you’d state in an interview?
cards.back: Sliding window is for contiguous subarrays/substrings under a constraint (max sum of k, longest substring without repeats): expand the right edge, shrink the left while the constraint is violated — O(n) because each element enters and leaves once.

cards.front: Why is ‘use a hash map’ the most common interview unlock?
cards.back: It trades space for time: O(1) average lookups turn O(n²) pair-searches into O(n) single passes — two-sum, frequency counts, memoization keys, and seen-sets all run on this trade.

cards.front: What do prefix sums buy you in an interview?
cards.back: O(1) range-sum queries after O(n) preprocessing: subarray sums become prefix[j] − prefix[i−1], and ‘subarray summing to k’ becomes a hash map over prefix values — the standard follow-up when brute force is O(n²).

cards.front: When does a monotonic stack appear in interviews?
cards.back: ‘Next greater element’ and histogram-rectangle problems: the stack keeps candidates in increasing order, and each element is pushed and popped once — O(n) for problems that look O(n²).

quiz.q: Pattern-recognition drilling works because interviews test:
choices: Mapping novel problems to known patterns under time pressure
quiz.explain: You’ll never see the exact problem again — but you’ll see the pattern.

quiz.q: A monotonic stack solves ‘next greater element’ in O(n) because:
choices: Each element is pushed and popped at most once
quiz.explain: Amortized O(1) work per element: once popped, an element never re-enters the stack.

quiz.q: With prefix[k] = sum of arr[0..k], the sum of arr[i..j] is:
quiz.explain: Subtract the sum before i from the sum through j; what remains is exactly arr[i..j].

quiz.q: A hash map reduces two-sum from O(n²) to O(n) because:
choices: Each complement lookup becomes O(1) average
quiz.explain: For each x, checking whether target−x was seen is one hash lookup instead of a full rescan.

cards.front: How do you reason about recursion out loud in an interview?
cards.back: State the base case first, then the recursive step’s contract: ‘assume it works for n−1, here’s how I build n.’ Then name the call-stack cost — depth × frame size — because interviewers probe stack depth and overflow.

cards.front: In-order, pre-order, post-order — how do you keep them straight under pressure?
cards.back: It’s about when you visit the node relative to its children: pre = before, in = between (gives sorted order on a BST), post = after (children before parent — natural for deletion and bottom-up computations).

cards.front: What’s the BST invariant, and why do interviewers care?
cards.back: ‘Left subtree < node < right subtree’ at every node. It buys O(log n) search/insert/delete when balanced — and the follow-up is always about what breaks it: degenerate insertion order gives O(n) without balancing.

cards.front: Heap vs sorted array: how do you justify a heap in an interview?
cards.back: When you need the min/max repeatedly but not full order: push/pop in O(log n), peek in O(1). Top-k, merge-k-sorted, and streaming medians are heap problems — say ‘I need repeated access to the extreme, not a full sort.’

cards.front: How do you represent graphs in interviews?
cards.back: Adjacency lists by default: O(V+E) memory, fast neighbor iteration — the right choice for sparse graphs (which interview graphs are). Adjacency matrix only for dense graphs or O(1) edge queries. The interview line: ‘list unless I can say why matrix.’

quiz.q: Shortest path in an unweighted graph is a BFS problem because:
choices: BFS explores in increasing distance from the source
quiz.explain: BFS’s level order guarantees the first time you reach a node is via the fewest edges.

quiz.q: Adjacency lists beat matrices for typical interview graphs because:
choices: O(V+E) memory and fast neighbor iteration on sparse graphs
quiz.explain: Interview graphs are sparse; matrices would waste O(V²) on empty edges.

quiz.q: Finding the k largest elements in a stream is a heap problem because:
choices: A min-heap of size k keeps the k largest with O(log k) updates
quiz.explain: Keep a min-heap of the k best seen; each new element is compared against the heap top in O(log k).

quiz.q: A BST built by inserting the sorted keys 1..n degenerates to:
choices: A linked list with O(n) operations
quiz.explain: Each insertion goes right every time; height becomes n and the log-n guarantee evaporates.

notes.body:

cards.front: What’s the first thing you write for a DP problem?
cards.back: The recurrence in words, before any code: ‘dp[i] = …’ stated as a decision — e.g. ‘rob or skip house i.’ Interviewers score the recurrence; the code is transcription. Then name the overlapping subproblems that make memoization valid.

cards.front: Memoization vs tabulation: how do you compare them in an interview?
cards.back: Same complexity, different direction: memoization is top-down recursion + cache (natural to write, pays recursion overhead); tabulation is bottom-up iteration (no stack risk, often better constants). State both, pick one, justify.

cards.front: What’s the 1D DP ladder?
cards.back: The progression: climbing stairs (dp[i] = dp[i-1] + dp[i-2]) → house robber (add the skip-or-take decision) → harder 1D problems. Master the ladder and every 1D DP is a variation — the interview line: ‘I climb the ladder before I attempt the roof.’

cards.front: How do you recognize a knapsack problem in disguise?
cards.back: ‘Choose a subset under a capacity to maximize value’ — partition-equal-subset, coin change, and target-sum are all knapsack variants. Name the pattern out loud: ‘this is 0/1 knapsack on capacity W,’ then write the recurrence.

cards.front: LCS and edit distance: what’s the shared DP skeleton?
cards.back: A 2D table over the two strings’ prefixes: dp[i][j] from dp[i−1][j], dp[i][j−1], dp[i−1][j−1]. Match → extend the diagonal; mismatch → take the best neighbor. Say ‘prefixes table’ and the interviewer knows you see it.

quiz.q: Good DP state design means the state:
choices: Captures exactly the information needed to make future decisions — no more, no less
quiz.explain: Too little state and the recurrence can’t decide; too much and you blow up the table for nothing.

quiz.q: In edit distance, dp[i][j] represents:
choices: The min edits to convert the first i chars of A to the first j chars of B
quiz.explain: The prefixes-table framing: every cell solves the subproblem on the two prefixes.

quiz.q: The 0/1 knapsack decision at each item is:
choices: Take it or skip it, respecting remaining capacity
quiz.explain: The 0/1 constraint forces a binary choice per item: dp[i][w] = max(skip, take).

quiz.q: House robber’s recurrence dp[i] = max(dp[i-1], dp[i-2] + nums[i]) encodes:
choices: The skip-or-take decision at each house
quiz.explain: Each house: skip it (dp[i-1]) or rob it plus the best up to i-2.

cards.front: How do you open a system design round?
cards.back: Requirements before architecture: restate functional requirements (what the system does), then non-functional (scale, latency, availability, consistency). Scoping first proves you design the right system — candidates who draw boxes before asking get failed.

cards.front: What are interviewers actually testing with back-of-envelope estimation?
cards.back: Order-of-magnitude judgment, not arithmetic: powers of 10 for users, QPS, storage, and bandwidth, with stated assumptions. Round aggressively, narrate the assumptions, and drive toward a design decision (shard? cache? CDN?).

cards.front: Load balancer, cache, CDN — the one-line job of each?
cards.back: Load balancer: spread traffic across healthy servers. Cache: serve hot data without hitting the origin (Redis/Memcached). CDN: push static content to the edge near users. In a design, place them in that order along the request path.

cards.front: SQL vs NoSQL: how do you ‘choose honestly’ in an interview?
cards.back: Name the workload, not the hype: need joins, transactions, and flexible queries → relational; massive write scale, simple key access, flexible schema → NoSQL family by access pattern (document, key-value, wide-column). The honest answer always starts from the access patterns.

cards.front: How do you discuss CAP without reciting the textbook?
cards.back: ‘During a network partition, I choose between consistency and availability — and here’s which my system needs and why.’ Then name the real tradeoff in your design: e.g. ‘the feed can be eventually consistent, but payments cannot.’

quiz.q: CAP says a distributed system under partition must sacrifice:
quiz.explain: Partitions are a fact of networks; the choice is CP (consistent, unavailable) or AP (available, inconsistent).

quiz.q: The deciding factor in SQL vs NoSQL should be:
choices: The data’s access patterns and consistency needs
quiz.explain: Storage choice follows how data is read and written and what consistency the product needs.

quiz.q: A CDN primarily reduces:
choices: Latency for static content by serving from edge locations
quiz.explain: Edge caches put bytes near users; origin round-trips disappear for cacheable content.

quiz.q: 100M daily active users making 10 requests each ≈ what average QPS?
quiz.explain: 100M × 10 = 10⁹ requests/day ÷ 86,400 s/day ≈ 11,574 — roughly 12k QPS.

cards.front: Walk the URL-shortener design in 60 seconds.
cards.back: Requirements (shorten + redirect, scale), estimation, API (POST /shorten, GET /{id} → 301), ID generation (counter vs hash, base62), storage (key-value, cache hot URLs), scaling (shard by hash, CDN for redirects).

cards.front: How do you structure the rate-limiter design answer?
cards.back: Requirements (limit per user/IP, burst policy), algorithm choice (token bucket for bursts, leaky bucket for smoothing — say which and why), distributed state (Redis with Lua for atomicity), and headers communicating limits to clients.

cards.front: How do you design a notification service in an interview?
cards.back: Requirements (channels: push/email/SMS, ordering, dedup), estimation (fan-out math), queue-based workers per channel with retries and DLQs, templates service, rate limits per provider, and idempotency so retries don’t double-notify.

cards.front: What goes in the one-page design doc?
cards.back: Requirements and constraints, the architecture sketch, API and data model, scaling math, failure modes, and open tradeoffs — one page forces decisions. Interviewers score whether the doc could actually guide a build.

cards.front: How do you present a design in 45 minutes?
cards.back: Timebox: 5 min requirements, 5 estimation, 10 API/data, 15 deep-dive on the hard part, 10 tradeoffs/failures/Q&A. End with ‘here are the three tradeoffs I’d revisit with more time’ — it shows judgment and invites the discussion interviewers want.

quiz.q: A review rubric’s value is:
choices: Comparable, complete feedback — every design judged on the same axes
quiz.explain: Fixed axes prevent reviews from fixating on one pet concern.

quiz.q: Ending a design round with open tradeoffs is strong because:
choices: It shows judgment about what matters and invites collaborative discussion
quiz.explain: Naming what you’d revisit proves you see the design’s limits — a senior signal.

quiz.q: A design doc’s failure-modes section exists to:
choices: Show you’ve thought about what breaks and how the system degrades — the senior signal
quiz.explain: Anyone can draw the happy path; naming failure modes and mitigations proves operational thinking.

quiz.q: Notification workers are typically queue-based because:
choices: Bursty send volume decouples from provider rate limits — workers drain at a sustainable pace with retries
quiz.explain: Queues absorb spikes and give retry/DLQ semantics per channel; direct calls would collapse under bursts.

cards.front: How do you handle the 30-minute coding bar?
cards.back: Budget aloud: 5 min clarify + plan, 20 min code, 5 min test. Start with brute force stated and its complexity (it buys time and shows honesty), then optimize the bottleneck. A working brute force beats a half-written optimal.

cards.front: What’s the standard system-design walkthrough?
cards.back: Requirements → estimation → API → data model → happy-path design → scaling/bottlenecks → failure modes → tradeoffs summary. Drive with questions, think aloud, and treat the interviewer as a collaborator, not an examiner.

cards.front: What’s the STAR structure, and why does it work for behavioral rounds?
cards.back: Situation (2 sentences of context), Task (your responsibility), Action (what YOU did — the bulk), Result (measurable outcome + lesson). It works because interviewers score evidence of behavior, and STAR forces a complete evidence unit.

cards.front: What makes a mock interview actually improve you?
cards.back: The debrief loop: within an hour, write what leaked (fumbled complexity? silent coding? weak STAR?), pick the single biggest leak, and redrill it within 48 hours. Mocks without debriefs are just stage fright practice.

cards.front: What’s the final two-week taper?
cards.back: Stop learning new topics; redrill weak patterns from your debrief log, run full timed mocks, fix sleep, and rehearse your story bank aloud. The taper converts knowledge into performance — cramming new material now only adds noise.

quiz.q: The taper period’s rule is:
choices: No new material — redrill weak spots, mock timed, rest
quiz.explain: Performance comes from consolidation and recovery, not last-minute breadth.

quiz.q: The highest-value activity right after a mock is:
choices: A written debrief naming what leaked, plus a redrill plan
quiz.explain: Improvement comes from the feedback loop: name the leak, target the redrill, verify next time.

quiz.q: In a STAR answer, the ‘A’ should emphasize:
quiz.explain: ‘We’ stories hide your contribution — interviewers evaluate you, so make your decisions explicit.

quiz.q: In a design round, the interviewer is best treated as:
choices: A collaborator — ask questions, incorporate feedback, design together
quiz.explain: Design rounds simulate real design work: collaborative, iterative, tradeoff-driven.

cards.front: What makes an API ‘RESTful’ in an interview answer?
cards.back: Resources as nouns in URLs, HTTP verbs as actions, status codes as the contract (200/201/400/401/403/404/429/500), stateless requests, and versioning — then the judgment calls: pagination, filtering, and idempotency.

cards.front: How do you explain idempotency to an interviewer?
cards.back: ‘Safe to retry’: repeating the request doesn’t change the outcome beyond the first application. Design it with idempotency keys on writes, and pair it with safe retries (exponential backoff + jitter) for distributed calls.

cards.front: Offset vs cursor pagination: the interview-ready comparison?
cards.back: Offset is simple but skips/duplicates rows when data changes and gets slower deep into the list; cursor (keyset) pagination is stable and O(1)-ish per page using an indexed column. Choose cursor for feeds, offset for admin UIs.

cards.front: When do queries beat endpoints — your GraphQL judgment call?
cards.back: When clients need varied, nested data and over/under-fetching hurts (mobile, aggregations): one query, exact fields, typed schema. The costs you must name: caching is harder, query complexity needs limits, and N+1 resolvers need batching (dataloaders).

cards.front: When is gRPC the right answer?
cards.back: Service-to-service inside the trust boundary: binary protobufs (fast, small), strict contracts via .proto, and streaming RPCs. The tradeoff: poor browser support and harder debugging than JSON — so internal microservices yes, public APIs usually no.

quiz.q: A good API error response includes a request ID so that:
choices: Support can correlate the client’s error with server-side logs
quiz.explain: Correlation IDs connect the client’s report to the exact server-side trace.

quiz.q: gRPC’s contract-first design means:
choices: Services share .proto definitions so clients and servers stay in sync
quiz.explain: The .proto file is the single source of truth generating typed clients and servers.

quiz.q: GraphQL’s main cost vs REST that you must name in an interview is:
choices: Caching and rate-limiting are harder without per-endpoint semantics
quiz.explain: A single endpoint with arbitrary query shapes defeats HTTP caching and simple per-route limits — you need query-cost analysis.

quiz.q: Cursor pagination avoids the ‘missing rows’ problem of offset because:
choices: It pages relative to a stable key instead of a shifting row number
quiz.explain: New inserts shift offsets; a keyset cursor anchors to the last seen key, immune to shifts.

cards.front: How do you discuss schema design and normalization?
cards.back: Normalize to remove redundancy (1NF→2NF→3NF: atomic values, no partial or transitive dependencies), then denormalize deliberately where read performance demands it — documenting why. The interview line: ‘normalize by default, denormalize by measurement.’

cards.front: How do you explain indexes in a backend interview?
cards.back: B-tree indexes turn O(n) scans into O(log n) lookups on the indexed columns — at the cost of write overhead and storage. Composite indexes serve multi-column filters left-to-right; covering indexes answer the query without touching the table.

cards.front: How do you talk about transaction isolation levels?
cards.back: The ladder: read uncommitted → read committed → repeatable read → serializable, trading anomalies (dirty reads, non-repeatable reads, phantoms) for concurrency. Name the anomaly your workload can’t tolerate, then pick the level.

cards.front: Name the NoSQL families and their fit in one breath.
cards.back: Document (flexible JSON, e.g. product catalogs), key-value (blazing simple lookups, sessions/caches), wide-column (massive write scale, time series), graph (relationship-heavy traversals). Fit follows access pattern.

cards.front: What’s the N+1 query problem and its fix?
cards.back: Loading N parents then one query per parent’s children: N+1 round trips. The fix is eager loading — a JOIN or batched second query (and ORMs have explicit eager-loading APIs). Name it when you see loops over queries.

quiz.q: The expand-contract migration pattern’s core idea is:
choices: Backward-compatible steps where old and new code coexist
quiz.explain: Every intermediate state must work with both old and new code; the old shape is removed only after readers move.

quiz.q: Eager loading fixes N+1 by:
choices: Fetching related rows in bulk (JOIN or batched query) instead of one query per parent
quiz.explain: One bulk fetch replaces N per-row queries; round trips collapse from N+1 to ~2.

quiz.q: A shopping-cart session store is a natural key-value fit because:
choices: Access is by a single session key with simple read/write
quiz.explain: Single-key access with no relations is exactly the key-value sweet spot.

quiz.q: Repeatable read prevents ___ but still allows ___:
quiz.explain: Repeatable read holds read locks so re-reads are stable, but new rows matching the predicate (phantoms) can still appear.

cards.front: Cache-aside vs read-through vs write-through?
cards.back: Cache-aside: app checks cache, falls back to DB, populates cache (flexible, stale-risk). Read-through: cache loads from DB itself. Write-through: writes go to cache and DB together (consistent, slower writes). Name the invalidation story for whichever you pick.

cards.front: What’s the thundering herd, and how do you stop it?
cards.back: A hot cache key expires and every request stampedes the DB at once. Fixes: request coalescing (single-flight — one request loads, others wait), probabilistic early refresh, or staggered TTLs with jitter.

cards.front: Why does Redis show up in backend interviews constantly?
cards.back: Because it’s five tools in one: strings (counters, rate limits), hashes (objects), lists (queues), sets (unique membership), sorted sets (leaderboards, time-ordered feeds) — all in-memory with persistence options. Name the structure that fits the access pattern.

cards.front: At-least-once vs exactly-once: the honest interview answer?
cards.back: At-least-once is the practical default (retries can duplicate); exactly-once needs idempotent consumers or transactions (Kafka EOS). The strong answer: ‘I design consumers idempotent, so duplicates are harmless — then at-least-once delivery is effectively exactly-once processing.’

cards.front: Kafka in 60 seconds for an interview.
cards.back: Distributed commit log: topics split into partitions (the parallelism unit), producers append, consumer groups split partitions across consumers, offsets track progress. Choose it for durable event streaming with replay — and name the ordering guarantee: per-partition only.

quiz.q: A bounded queue with a drop-or-block policy implements:
choices: Backpressure — the producer feels the consumer’s slowness
quiz.explain: Bounded buffers propagate slowness upstream instead of growing memory until collapse.

quiz.q: In Kafka, ordering is guaranteed:
quiz.explain: A partition is an append-only log — total order holds inside it, not across partitions.

quiz.q: The most robust way to handle duplicate deliveries is:
choices: Preventing all duplicates in the broker
Idempotent consumers, so reprocessing is safe
quiz.explain: Duplicates are inevitable in distributed systems; idempotency makes them harmless.

quiz.q: A leaderboard is a natural Redis sorted-set fit because:
choices: Members are ordered by score with O(log n) updates and range queries
quiz.explain: Sorted sets keep members ordered by score: rank lookups and top-N ranges are native operations.

cards.front: Threads vs processes vs event loops?
cards.back: Processes: isolated memory, expensive. Threads: shared memory, cheap-ish, need locks. Event loop: single-threaded async I/O (Node, asyncio) — great for I/O-bound, terrible for CPU-bound. Match the model to the bottleneck.

cards.front: How do you explain deadlock prevention?
cards.back: Deadlock needs four conditions (mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, circular wait) — break any one: lock ordering (always acquire in the same global order) is the classic fix. In an interview, draw the wait cycle, then name the broken condition.

cards.front: What is backpressure, and where do you put it?
cards.back: When consumers are slower than producers, pressure must go somewhere: bounded queues that block/shed, reactive streams with demand signaling, or Kafka consumer-lag alerting. The interview point: an unbounded queue is a deferred outage.

cards.front: Token bucket vs leaky bucket — which allows bursts?
cards.back: Token bucket: tokens accumulate up to capacity, so short bursts above the sustained rate are allowed. Leaky bucket: requests queue and drain at a constant rate — smooth output, no bursts. State which behavior the product needs.

cards.front: Why is distributed locking hard, and what’s the Redis answer?
cards.back: Locks must survive holder crashes (TTL/lease) and clock issues; naive SETNX without expiry deadlocks on crash. The pattern: SET with NX + PX expiry, fencing tokens for ordering, and always keep the critical section short.

quiz.q: An idempotent pipeline stage guarantees:
choices: Reprocessing the same input produces the same output — no duplicates
quiz.explain: Reruns are inevitable; idempotency makes them safe.

quiz.q: A distributed lock MUST have an expiry because:
choices: A crashed holder would otherwise hold the lock forever
quiz.explain: Without TTL, a holder that dies mid-section deadlocks every waiter — the lease bounds the damage.

quiz.q: An API that should allow brief traffic spikes should use:
quiz.explain: Accumulated tokens absorb bursts up to bucket capacity; a leaky bucket would queue or drop them.

quiz.q: A bounded queue with a drop-or-block policy implements:
choices: Backpressure — the producer feels the consumer’s slowness
quiz.explain: Bounded buffers propagate slowness upstream instead of growing memory until collapse.

cards.front: How do you decompose a monolith in a design interview?
cards.back: By bounded contexts (DDD): split along business capabilities with clean ownership, not technical layers. Each service owns its data; cross-service needs go through APIs or events. And name the honest counterargument: start modular-monolith until the seams are proven.

cards.front: Sync vs async service communication?
cards.back: Sync (REST/gRPC): simple, but couples availability and latency — a slow downstream slows you. Async (queues/events): decoupled, resilient, but eventual consistency and harder debugging. The interview line: ‘sync for queries needing answers now, async for work that can wait.’

cards.front: What do service discovery and API gateways do?
cards.back: Service discovery: services find each other’s current addresses as instances churn (registry or DNS-based). API gateway: single entry point handling routing, auth, rate limiting, and aggregation for clients.

cards.front: Distributed transactions: what’s the saga answer?
cards.back: No 2PC across services — use sagas: a sequence of local transactions where each step has a compensating action (refund, cancel) for rollback. Choreography (events) for simple flows, orchestration (a saga coordinator) when the flow needs central control.

cards.front: Logs, metrics, traces — when do you reach for each?
cards.back: Metrics: ‘is something wrong’ (alerts, dashboards). Logs: ‘what happened’ (discrete events with context). Traces: ‘where did the request go’ (latency across services). The interview line: ‘metrics alert me, traces show me where, logs tell me why.’

quiz.q: A modular monolith is often the right starting point because:
choices: It keeps bounded-context discipline without paying the distributed-systems tax prematurely
quiz.explain: Distribution is a cost; pay it when a proven seam demands independent scaling or ownership.

quiz.q: A distributed trace’s primary value is:
choices: Following one request across services to find where latency/errors originate
quiz.explain: Trace spans stitch the request path across service boundaries — the only view that crosses them.

quiz.q: A saga handles failure of step 3 in a 5-step flow by:
quiz.explain: Each completed step’s compensating transaction semantically undoes it — the distributed answer to rollback.

quiz.q: An API gateway centralizes:
choices: Cross-cutting edge concerns: routing, auth, rate limiting for inbound traffic
quiz.explain: One policy-enforcement point at the edge beats reimplementing auth and limits in every service.

cards.front: How do you design a rate-limited public API?
cards.back: Requirements (limits per key/IP, burst policy) → token-bucket in Redis with atomic Lua → 429 + RateLimit-* headers + Retry-After → per-endpoint tiers. The interview line: ‘the limiter is part of the API contract, not an afterthought.’

cards.front: How do you design an order pipeline with queues?
cards.back: API accepts and validates → order events to a queue → workers for payment, inventory, notification (each with retries + DLQ) → saga/compensation for failures. The interview line: ‘the queue is the seam where reliability lives.’

cards.front: What goes in an API contract / OpenAPI sketch?
cards.back: Endpoints, methods, request/response schemas, status codes, error model, auth, rate limits, and versioning — enough that a client team could build against it. The interview line: ‘the contract is the interface; code is the implementation.’

cards.front: k6 vs JMeter — how do you compare them?
cards.back: k6: JS-scripted, developer-friendly, great for CI-integrated load tests with thresholds as gates. JMeter: GUI-driven, mature, huge protocol support, heavier. The interview line: ‘k6 for code-reviewed load tests in the pipeline; JMeter where the team already lives in it.’

cards.front: What goes in a failure-mode writeup?
cards.back: For each component: how it fails, blast radius, detection (which alert fires), mitigation (what the responder does), and whether degradation is graceful. The interview line: ‘I design the unhappy path with the same care as the happy one.’

quiz.q: Ending a design round with open tradeoffs is strong because:
choices: It shows judgment about what matters and invites collaborative discussion
quiz.explain: Naming what you’d revisit proves you see the design’s limits — a senior signal.

quiz.q: A failure-mode writeup’s audience is:
choices: The future on-call responder — it’s a pre-written triage guide
quiz.explain: Written calmly now, it guides panicked decisions at 3am.

quiz.q: k6’s thresholds turn a load test into:
choices: A gate: breaching p95/error-rate assertions fails the run
quiz.explain: Thresholds are pass/fail assertions on metrics — the test proves the SLO or it fails.

quiz.q: Writing the contract before the implementation is strong because:
choices: It forces interface decisions early, when they’re cheap — and enables parallel client/server work
quiz.explain: Contract-first surfaces disagreements before code cements them.

cards.front: How do you survive concurrency + data-layer deep dives?

cards.front: What makes a mock interview actually improve you?

cards.front: What’s the final two-week taper?

cards.front: Explain closures like the interviewer is testing depth.
cards.back: A function that captures variables from its enclosing scope — the variables live as long as the closure does. That’s the module pattern, private state, and also the classic bug: loop variables captured by reference (fixed with let in modern JS).

cards.front: How do you explain ‘this’ and prototypes without rambling?
cards.back: ‘this’ is set by the call site (method call, plain call, new, arrow functions inherit lexically). Prototypes are the delegation chain: property lookup walks up the chain. Classes are syntax over the same prototype mechanism.

cards.front: Microtasks vs macrotasks — the interview-ready version?
cards.back: The event loop drains the microtask queue (promises, queueMicrotask) completely after each macrotask (setTimeout, I/O, rendering steps). So promise callbacks run before setTimeout(0) — and a microtask loop can starve rendering.

cards.front: What do interviewers probe in promises/async-await?
cards.back: Error paths: unhandled rejections, try/catch around await, Promise.all failing fast vs allSettled for independent work, and never mixing raw callbacks with await. The senior signal: ‘here’s how this fails and how the caller learns about it.’

cards.front: What TypeScript features do interviewers actually ask about?
cards.back: Narrowing (typeof/instanceof/discriminated unions — exhaustiveness checking with never), generics with constraints, and utility types (Partial, Pick, Omit, Record). The pitch: ‘types as executable documentation that the compiler checks.’

quiz.q: Rehearsing the perennial questions pays off because:
choices: They’re guaranteed points — fluency here buys composure for the novel problems
quiz.explain: Banking the predictable questions preserves mental budget for the unpredictable ones.

quiz.q: A discriminated union’s power in TypeScript is:
choices: Exhaustive narrowing: the compiler proves you handled every variant
quiz.explain: Switching on the discriminant literal lets TS narrow each branch — and ‘never’ in default proves exhaustiveness.

quiz.q: Promise.all vs Promise.allSettled: the difference is:
choices: all rejects on the first rejection; allSettled waits for every outcome
quiz.explain: all short-circuits on first failure; allSettled reports each promise’s fulfilled/rejected status.

quiz.q: Promise.then callbacks run before setTimeout(0) callbacks because:
quiz.explain: The spec processes the entire microtask queue after each macrotask — promises always win the race.

cards.front: What does ‘components as functions of state’ mean?
cards.back: UI = f(state): given the same state, the component renders the same output — no hidden dependencies. It’s why unidirectional data flow works and why testing components is easy: set state, assert output. The interview line: ‘pure rendering functions; side effects at the edges.’

cards.front: Explain closures like the interviewer is testing depth.
cards.back: A function that captures variables from its enclosing scope — the variables live as long as the closure does. That’s the module pattern, private state, and also the classic bug: loop variables captured by reference (fixed with let in modern JS).

cards.front: Why do keys matter in React lists?
cards.back: Reconciliation matches old and new elements by key: stable keys let React move/reuse DOM nodes; index keys on reorderable lists cause wrong state reuse and wasted re-renders. Keys are identity, not decoration.

cards.front: memo, useMemo, useCallback — when is each the right call?
cards.back: memo: skip re-rendering a component when props are shallow-equal (for expensive subtrees). useMemo: cache an expensive computation. useCallback: stabilize a function identity passed to memoized children. And the caveat: don’t memoize everything — measure first.

cards.front: How do you discuss state management tradeoffs?
cards.back: Lift state to the lowest common parent first; context for truly global low-churn data (theme, auth) — not as a state manager, since context re-renders all consumers; external stores (Zustand/Redux) for complex shared state with selective subscriptions.

quiz.q: React Server Components primarily reduce:
choices: Client-side JavaScript shipped for non-interactive UI
quiz.explain: Server-rendered components never hydrate: their code stays off the client bundle.

quiz.q: React context is a poor state manager for high-churn state because:
choices: Every consumer re-renders on any context value change
quiz.explain: Context has no selectors: one value change re-renders all consumers regardless of what they use.

quiz.q: useCallback’s purpose is:
choices: Preserving function identity across renders so memoized children don’t re-render
quiz.explain: A new function identity each render defeats memo on children; useCallback stabilizes it.

quiz.q: Using array index as key breaks when:
choices: Items reorder or are inserted — React reuses the wrong component state
quiz.explain: Identity must follow the item, not its position; index keys lie about identity on reorder.

cards.front: Walk the critical rendering path.
cards.back: Parse HTML → build DOM, parse CSS → CSSOM, combine → render tree, layout (positions/sizes), paint, composite. Anything blocking (sync scripts, render-blocking CSS) delays first paint — that’s why script placement and resource hints matter.

cards.front: Reflow vs repaint vs compositing?
cards.back: Reflow (layout): geometry changes — expensive, cascades. Repaint: visual changes without geometry. Compositing: GPU layer moves (transform/opacity) — cheapest. The perf rule: animate transform and opacity only; batch DOM reads/writes to avoid layout thrash.

cards.front: LCP, INP, CLS — what does each measure?
cards.back: LCP (Largest Contentful Paint): loading — when the main content appears. INP (Interaction to Next Paint): responsiveness — worst-case input latency. CLS (Cumulative Layout Shift): visual stability — unexpected movement. For all three, lower is better.

cards.front: How do you profile with DevTools Performance?
cards.back: Record an interaction, read the flame chart: long tasks, layout/paint blocks, and JS call stacks. Find the bottleneck first (scripting? rendering? network?), fix that, re-measure. The interview line: ‘profile before optimizing — otherwise you’re guessing.’

cards.front: How do you justify code splitting in a perf interview?
cards.back: Ship only what the route needs: route-level splits plus lazy-loading below-the-fold/heavy components cut initial JS, which cuts parse/compile time — the real mobile bottleneck. Measure with coverage/devtools before and after.

quiz.q: prefetch differs from preload in that:
choices: prefetch is low-priority for likely-future navigations; preload is high-priority for the current page
quiz.explain: Priority and intent differ: current-page critical vs next-navigation likely.

quiz.q: Code splitting improves load performance mainly by:
choices: Reducing initial JavaScript parsed and executed
quiz.explain: Initial bundle size drives parse/compile cost; splitting defers non-critical code.

quiz.q: The first step of any performance investigation is:
choices: Profiling to find the actual bottleneck
quiz.explain: Optimizing without measurement optimizes the wrong thing; the flame chart decides.

quiz.q: A high CLS score means:
choices: The page visibly jumps around as content loads — poor visual stability
quiz.explain: CLS sums unexpected layout shifts; late-loading content pushing text around is the classic cause.

cards.front: Box model and specificity in 30 seconds?
cards.back: Content + padding + border + margin; box-sizing: border-box makes widths sane. Specificity: inline > ID > class > element; the cascade resolves ties by source order. Keep specificity flat (BEM/utilities) so overrides stay predictable.

cards.front: Flexbox vs Grid: the choosing rule?
cards.back: Flexbox for one-dimensional layout (a row or column of items, content-driven sizing). Grid for two-dimensional layout (rows AND columns, explicit placement). Most real UIs compose both.

cards.front: How do you discuss responsive design modernly?
cards.back: Fluid layouts + breakpoints for viewport adaptation, container queries for component-level responsiveness (the component adapts to its container, not the viewport). The interview line: ‘viewport queries adapt pages; container queries adapt components.’

cards.front: How do you keep CSS maintainable at scale?
cards.back: Architecture with flat specificity: BEM naming (block__element--modifier), CSS modules for scoping, or utility classes — pick one and enforce it. The interview line: ‘specificity wars are a process failure, not a CSS failure.’

cards.front: What’s the transform-and-opacity discipline?
cards.back: Animate only transform and opacity: they composite on the GPU without layout or paint. Animating width/left/top triggers reflow — jank. The interview line: ‘if it moves pixels through layout, it’s not an animation, it’s a slideshow.’

quiz.q: Using a <div> with onClick instead of <button> harms accessibility because:
choices: It loses built-in keyboard support, focus, and screen-reader semantics
quiz.explain: Native controls carry keyboard handling and ARIA roles for free; divs need all of it rebuilt.

quiz.q: A janky animation’s usual cause is:
choices: Animating layout-triggering properties instead of transform/opacity
quiz.explain: Layout per frame blows the 16ms budget; composited properties don’t.

quiz.q: BEM’s naming discipline prevents:
choices: Specificity wars — flat, predictable selectors instead of deep nesting
quiz.explain: block__element--modifier keeps every selector at one class of specificity: overrides stay sane.

quiz.q: Container queries improve on media queries by:
choices: Letting components respond to their container’s size — reusable in any layout
quiz.explain: Component-level responsiveness: the same card works in a sidebar and a full page.

cards.front: How do you structure the ‘design a news feed’ answer?
cards.back: Requirements (post, follow, ranked feed), API, data model (posts, edges), fan-out: push for normal users, pull for celebrities (the famous hybrid), ranking separate from delivery, cache hot feeds, pagination.

cards.front: Design typeahead/autocomplete: the key decisions?
cards.back: Debounce input (~200–300ms), prefix index (trie or indexed prefix column), rank by popularity/recency, cache hot prefixes aggressively. Client: cancel stale in-flight requests so slow responses don’t overwrite fresh ones.

cards.front: How do you design a photo gallery at scale?
cards.back: Upload → object storage → async thumbnails (multiple sizes) → CDN in front → lazy loading + responsive images (srcset) on the client. The interview line: ‘bytes are the budget — every decision serves fewer, smaller, closer bytes.’

cards.front: How do you handle client-side caching and state sync?
cards.back: Normalize server data in a client cache (React Query/SWR style): stale-while-revalidate for freshness, cache keys as query keys, optimistic updates with rollback on error, and invalidation tied to mutations. The interview line: ‘the server is the truth; the client cache is a performance layer with an eviction policy.’

cards.front: Polling vs SSE vs WebSockets?
cards.back: Polling: simple, wasteful (empty responses). SSE: server→client stream over HTTP, auto-reconnect — perfect for notifications/feeds. WebSockets: full duplex — chat, games, collaboration. Choose the weakest tool that satisfies the direction and frequency.

quiz.q: A frontend design round emphasizes:
choices: Client architecture: state, caching/sync, rendering perf, real-time
quiz.explain: The graded system is the client: how it manages state, data, and performance at scale.

quiz.q: Server-Sent Events fit a live notification feed because:
choices: They’re a simple server-to-client stream with auto-reconnect — exactly the direction needed
quiz.explain: One-directional updates over plain HTTP: less machinery than WebSockets for the same job.

quiz.q: Stale-while-revalidate improves perceived performance by:
choices: Serving cached data instantly while revalidating in the background
quiz.explain: Instant render from cache, fresh data moments later — the best of both latencies.

quiz.q: Generating multiple thumbnail sizes at upload time is worth it because:
choices: Clients download exactly the size they display — no wasted bytes or client-side scaling
quiz.explain: Serve-the-right-size beats serve-one-size: bandwidth follows the display, not the source.

cards.front: What accessibility points score in frontend interviews?
cards.back: Semantic HTML first (buttons are <button>), visible focus states, color contrast, labels for inputs, alt text that conveys function, and keyboard operability. The line: ‘accessibility is a correctness requirement, tested like any other.’

cards.front: How do you approach a Kanban-with-drag-and-drop machine-coding task?

cards.front: How do you win a machine-coding round?

cards.front: How do you test a machine-coding build?

quiz.q: Testing Library prefers role-based queries because:

quiz.q: In machine coding, ‘working first’ means:

cards.front: Walk the request path: DNS to render.
cards.back: DNS resolve → TCP handshake → TLS → request hits CDN/edge → load balancer → app server → (cache → DB) → response → browser parses HTML/CSS/JS → render. Saying the full path out loud is the fullstack flex — then zoom into wherever the question points.

cards.front: Monolith vs modular monolith vs microservices?
cards.back: Monolith: one deployable, simplest ops. Modular monolith: bounded-context modules inside one deployable — the discipline without the distributed tax. Microservices: independent deployables — pay the distributed-systems cost only when seams demand it. The interview line: ‘I evolve toward distribution, I don’t start there.’

cards.front: What’s the BFF pattern?
cards.back: Backend-for-Frontend: a thin service per client type (web, mobile) that aggregates downstream microservices into exactly the shapes each UI needs — killing over-fetching without leaking service topology to clients.

cards.front: SSR vs SSG vs ISR?
cards.back: SSR: render per request (fresh, slower TTFB). SSG: render at build (fastest, stale until rebuild). ISR: static with timed revalidation (the middle path). Choose by freshness needs: marketing page → SSG; personalized dashboard → SSR.

cards.front: How do you reason about edge and CDN placement?
cards.back: Push static and cacheable dynamic content to the edge (CDN PoPs), compute at the edge only when latency demands it (edge functions), origin for the source of truth. The interview line: ‘every mile between the user and the byte is latency I can buy off.’

quiz.q: Drawing before diving deep is strong because:
choices: It establishes shared context — then both of you know where the deep dive lives
quiz.explain: The diagram is the map; deep dives are the territory. Maps first.

quiz.q: Edge computing earns its keep when:
choices: Latency is the constraint and the work is cacheable or lightweight per request
quiz.explain: Edge pays for latency-sensitive, lightweight work — not for heavy computation.

quiz.q: ISR’s advantage over pure SSG is:
choices: Pages revalidate in the background on an interval — fresh without rebuilds
quiz.explain: Stale-while-revalidate at the page level: serve cached, regenerate on schedule.

quiz.q: A BFF mainly solves:
choices: Over/under-fetching by shaping responses per client
quiz.explain: Each client gets an aggregation layer tuned to its screens instead of N chatty service calls.

cards.front: What makes an API ‘RESTful’ in an interview answer?
cards.back: Resources as nouns in URLs, HTTP verbs as actions, status codes as the contract (200/201/400/401/403/404/429/500), stateless requests, and versioning — then the judgment calls: pagination, filtering, and idempotency.

cards.front: When do queries beat endpoints — your GraphQL judgment call?
cards.back: When clients need varied, nested data and over/under-fetching hurts (mobile, aggregations): one query, exact fields, typed schema. The costs you must name: caching is harder, query complexity needs limits, and N+1 resolvers need batching (dataloaders).

cards.front: Over-fetching vs under-fetching — the honest comparison?
cards.back: Over-fetching: REST endpoints returning fields the client ignores (wasted bytes). Under-fetching: needing N requests for one screen (chatty). GraphQL fixes both per-query; the cost is caching complexity. The interview line: ‘I measure the waste before I prescribe the cure.’

cards.front: How do you discuss caching in a cloud interview?
cards.back: What to cache (read-heavy, slow-changing), where (CDN edge, app cache, DB query cache), invalidation strategy, and the failure story (thundering herd, stale reads). The interview line: ‘caching is a tradeoff with an invalidation plan, not a speedup.’

cards.front: Polling vs SSE vs WebSockets?
cards.back: Polling: simple, wasteful (empty responses). SSE: server→client stream over HTTP, auto-reconnect — perfect for notifications/feeds. WebSockets: full duplex — chat, games, collaboration. Choose the weakest tool that satisfies the direction and frequency.

quiz.q: Per-surface API choice is justified because:
choices: Client constraints differ (bandwidth, latency, capabilities) — the contract should fit the consumer
quiz.explain: The consumer’s constraints decide the contract shape, not architectural purity.

quiz.q: Server-Sent Events fit a live notification feed because:
choices: They’re a simple server-to-client stream with auto-reconnect — exactly the direction needed
quiz.explain: One-directional updates over plain HTTP: less machinery than WebSockets for the same job.

quiz.q: Every caching decision must name:
choices: The invalidation strategy — stale data is caching’s permanent tax
quiz.explain: Cache without an invalidation story is a future incident.

quiz.q: Under-fetching hurts mobile clients most because:
choices: Many sequential round trips compound on high-latency networks
quiz.explain: Chatty APIs multiply round-trip latency — the scarcest resource on mobile networks.

cards.front: Sessions vs tokens?
cards.back: Sessions: server-side state keyed by cookie — revocable instantly, needs sticky/shared store at scale. Tokens (JWT): stateless, self-contained — scales horizontally, but revocation needs denylists/short expiry. Choose by revocation needs.

cards.front: What’s inside a JWT, and what must you validate?
cards.back: Header.payload.signature, base64url: claims like sub, exp, iat. Validate: signature with the right key/algorithm (never ‘none’), expiry, issuer/audience. And the warning: JWTs are signed, not encrypted — never put secrets in claims.

cards.front: Walk the OAuth 2.0 authorization code flow.
cards.back: User → client redirects to auth server → user approves → auth code returned → client exchanges code (+ secret, PKCE for public clients) for tokens at the token endpoint. The code is short-lived and single-use; tokens never touch the browser URL.

cards.front: How do you store passwords — the interview answer?
cards.back: Never encrypt (reversible); hash with a memory-hard, salted function: Argon2id preferred, bcrypt acceptable. Per-user random salt, work factor tuned so login takes ~hundreds of ms. And never roll your own crypto.

cards.front: Which auth questions decide senior loops?
cards.back: ‘How do you revoke a JWT?’ (short expiry + denylist/rotation), ‘where do refresh tokens live?’ (httpOnly secure cookies, rotated), ‘how do you do SSO?’ (OIDC). The interview line: ‘I answer auth with threat models, not library names.’

quiz.q: JWT revocation’s honest answer is:
choices: Short-lived access tokens + refresh-token rotation and denylists — statelessness has a revocation cost
quiz.explain: Stateless tokens can’t be centrally killed; the design bounds the exposure window instead.

quiz.q: Passwords must be hashed, not encrypted, because:
choices: Encryption is reversible — a key leak exposes every password; hashing is one-way
quiz.explain: One-way hashing means even a full database theft doesn’t yield passwords (beyond cracking).

quiz.q: PKCE exists to protect:
choices: Public clients (mobile/SPA) that can’t keep a secret — the code exchange is bound to the original request
quiz.explain: Without a client secret, PKCE’s code_verifier/code_challenge pair prevents authorization-code interception.

quiz.q: A JWT is ___ not ___:
quiz.explain: Anyone can read the payload; the signature only proves it wasn’t tampered with.

- **SQLite Documentation** (https://www.sqlite.org/docs.html) — The embedded database every mobile and fullstack dev meets.

cards.front: ORMs vs query builders vs raw SQL?
cards.back: ORMs: speed of development, relationships as objects — watch N+1 and leaky abstraction on complex queries. Query builders: composable SQL without string soup. Raw SQL: full control for reporting/analytics. The senior line: ‘I use the ORM for CRUD and drop to SQL where it earns it.’

cards.front: How do you discuss full-text search basics?
cards.back: Inverted index: terms → documents, with tokenization, stemming, and ranking (TF-IDF/BM25). For interview depth: Postgres tsvector covers the simple case; dedicated engines (OpenSearch/Elasticsearch) earn their keep at scale, faceting, and relevance tuning.

cards.front: How do you handle file uploads at scale?
cards.back: Direct-to-object-storage uploads (presigned URLs — the app server never proxies bytes), async processing (thumbnails, virus scan) via queues, CDN in front for reads. The interview line: ‘bytes never touch my app servers.’

cards.front: How do you keep client cache and DB consistent?
cards.back: Server as source of truth; client cache as a performance layer with invalidation tied to mutations (optimistic updates + rollback on error, or refetch-on-mutation). The interview line: ‘the client cache is allowed to be wrong briefly, never permanently.’

cards.front: The interviewer asks you to go deep on 'From form to row: validation layers'. What answer structure makes you sound senior?
cards.back: Three beats: (1) one-sentence definition, (2) how it works mechanically, (3) when it fits and its key tradeoff — then stop and invite the follow-up. Structure is what separates a senior answer from a recitation.

quiz.q: Optimistic updates need a rollback path because:
choices: The server can reject the mutation — the UI must revert to truth
quiz.explain: Optimism is a UX bet; the rollback is the hedge when the bet loses.

quiz.q: Presigned URLs for uploads are preferred because:
choices: Clients upload straight to object storage — app servers never proxy the bytes
quiz.explain: Offloading byte transfer removes the app tier from the bandwidth path entirely.

quiz.q: An inverted index maps:
choices: Terms to the documents containing them — enabling fast keyword lookup
quiz.explain: Search flips the document: instead of scanning text, you look up precomputed term postings.

quiz.q: An ORM’s classic performance trap is:
choices: N+1 queries from lazy-loaded relationships in loops
quiz.explain: Accessing relations per-row in a loop fires a query each — eager loading is the fix.

- **Netlify Documentation** (https://docs.netlify.com/) — Deploys, forms, functions, and the frontend hosting model.

cards.front: What does a good CI/CD pipeline do?
cards.back: CI: every push builds, lints, tests, scans — fast feedback on main. CD: artifacts promoted through environments, deployments automated (blue-green/canary/rolling), rollback one command. The interview metrics: lead time and change-failure rate.

cards.front: Why do fullstack interviews love feature flags?
cards.back: They decouple deploy from release: merge dark code, release to 1%, kill-switch bad launches without redeploying. The discipline to name: flag hygiene — every flag gets an owner and a removal date, or you inherit flag spaghetti.

cards.front: What does Docker actually give you?
cards.back: A portable, reproducible runtime: the image bundles code + dependencies + OS userland, so ‘works on my machine’ dies. Containers share the host kernel (lighter than VMs, weaker isolation) — and the interview follow-up is always about image size and layer caching.

cards.front: Logs, metrics, traces — when do you reach for each?
cards.back: Metrics: ‘is something wrong’ (alerts, dashboards). Logs: ‘what happened’ (discrete events with context). Traces: ‘where did the request go’ (latency across services). The interview line: ‘metrics alert me, traces show me where, logs tell me why.’

cards.front: What’s a real rollback strategy?
cards.back: Deploy immutable artifacts, keep the previous version one command away (or N−1 running in blue-green), database migrations backward-compatible (expand-contract), and rehearse the rollback — an untested rollback plan is a hope.

quiz.q: Blue-green deployment’s rollback is:
choices: Instant: flip the router back to the still-running green environment
quiz.explain: The old environment stays live behind the router until cutover is verified — rollback is a route change.

quiz.q: A distributed trace’s primary value is:
choices: Following one request across services to find where latency/errors originate
quiz.explain: Trace spans stitch the request path across service boundaries — the only view that crosses them.

quiz.q: Containers differ from VMs in that they:
choices: Share the host OS kernel instead of virtualizing hardware
quiz.explain: No guest kernel per container: faster startup, denser packing, but a shared kernel attack surface.

quiz.q: Feature flags decouple:
choices: Deploying code from releasing features to users
quiz.explain: Code ships dark; the flag controls who sees it — enabling progressive rollout and instant kill-switches.

cards.front: How do you scope a shippable capstone app?

cards.front: What goes in an API contract / OpenAPI sketch?
cards.back: Endpoints, methods, request/response schemas, status codes, error model, auth, rate limits, and versioning — enough that a client team could build against it. The interview line: ‘the contract is the interface; code is the implementation.’

cards.front: What makes a capstone README and demo script work?

cards.front: How do you present a build in an interview?

cards.front: The interviewer asks you to go deep on 'Scoping a shippable app'. What answer structure makes you sound senior?

quiz.q: Ending with ‘what I’d do with more time’ is strong because:

quiz.q: An architecture diagram in the README is worth it because:
choices: Reviewers grasp the system in 30 seconds — before reading a line of code
quiz.explain: Hiring managers skim; the diagram carries the design when they won’t read prose.

quiz.q: Writing the contract before the implementation is strong because:
choices: It forces interface decisions early, when they’re cheap — and enables parallel client/server work
quiz.explain: Contract-first surfaces disagreements before code cements them.

quiz.q: API-contract-first in a capstone is strong because:
choices: It proves interface thinking and lets frontend/backend evolve independently

cards.front: How do you handle timed API-design rounds?
cards.back: Budget: 5 min requirements, 10 min resources + verbs + status codes, 10 min edge cases (pagination, idempotency, versioning), 5 min tradeoffs. Think in resources and contracts — the interview line: ‘I design the contract a client could program against.’

cards.front: What’s a behavioral ledger?
cards.back: Your running record: story bank entries, which stories you’ve told where, feedback received, and follow-up questions that stumped you. It stops you from repeating the same story and turns each behavioral round into training data.

cards.front: How do you debrief and triage after a mock?
cards.back: Within an hour, write what leaked (fumbled complexity? silent coding? weak STAR?), rank leaks by frequency × interview weight, and redrill the top one within 48 hours. The interview line: ‘the mock is the test; the debrief is the studying.’

cards.front: What’s the final two-week taper?
cards.back: Stop learning new topics; redrill weak patterns from your debrief log, run full timed mocks, fix sleep, and rehearse your story bank aloud. The taper converts knowledge into performance — cramming new material now only adds noise.

quiz.q: The taper period’s rule is:
choices: No new material — redrill weak spots, mock timed, rest
quiz.explain: Performance comes from consolidation and recovery, not last-minute breadth.

quiz.q: Weak-spot triage should prioritize leaks by:
choices: Frequency × interview weight — what costs the most points most often
quiz.explain: Expected value: fix what loses you the most points most often.

quiz.q: A behavioral ledger prevents:
choices: Repeating the same story across rounds and losing track of feedback
quiz.explain: Loops have multiple behavioral touchpoints; the ledger keeps each one fresh and improving.

quiz.q: In an API-design round, idempotency belongs in the discussion because:
choices: Clients retry — safe retries are a contract requirement, not an optimization

notes.body: - **Swift Documentation** (https://swift.org/documentation/) — The language guide and standard library reference.

cards.front: How do you show Optional mastery in a Swift interview?
cards.back: Binding (if let/guard let) over force-unwrapping, optional chaining for deep access, nil-coalescing for defaults, and ‘!!’ as a code smell you justify only with a proof. Map/flatMap on Optionals for transforms without pyramids.

cards.front: Value vs reference semantics — the Swift interview core?
cards.back: Structs/enums: copied on assignment (value semantics — no shared-state bugs). Classes: shared reference (identity matters: view controllers, shared services). Choose struct by default; reach for class when identity or inheritance is required.

cards.front: Why does Swift lean on protocols so hard?
cards.back: Protocol-oriented design: capabilities as protocols, shared behavior via protocol extensions with default implementations, generics constrained by protocols. The interview line: ‘prefer composition of protocols over class inheritance.’

cards.front: What TypeScript features do interviewers actually ask about?
cards.back: Narrowing (typeof/instanceof/discriminated unions — exhaustiveness checking with never), generics with constraints, and utility types (Partial, Pick, Omit, Record). The pitch: ‘types as executable documentation that the compiler checks.’

cards.front: Explain closures like the interviewer is testing depth.
cards.back: A function that captures variables from its enclosing scope — the variables live as long as the closure does. That’s the module pattern, private state, and also the classic bug: loop variables captured by reference (fixed with let in modern JS).

quiz.q: Using try! is acceptable only when:
choices: You can prove the call cannot fail (e.g. a bundled resource that ships with the app)
quiz.explain: try! converts failure into a crash — justifiable only with a proof, never with hope.

quiz.q: A closure lets a function:
choices: Access its outer scope’s variables after that scope has returned
quiz.explain: The captured environment outlives the enclosing call — that’s what makes private state possible.

quiz.q: A discriminated union’s power in TypeScript is:
choices: Exhaustive narrowing: the compiler proves you handled every variant
quiz.explain: Switching on the discriminant literal lets TS narrow each branch — and ‘never’ in default proves exhaustiveness.

quiz.q: Protocol extensions with default implementations enable:
choices: Shared behavior across conforming types without a base class
quiz.explain: Mixins via extensions: types gain behavior by conforming, no inheritance chain required.

cards.front: What must you know about UIViewController lifecycle?
cards.back: loadView → viewDidLoad (one-time setup) → viewWill/DidAppear (per-appearance work, start/stop observations) → viewWill/DidDisappear → deinit. The interview traps: doing per-appearance work in viewDidLoad, and leaking via unreleased observers.

cards.front: How do you discuss Auto Layout?
cards.back: Constraints as linear equations the solver satisfies; intrinsic content size vs explicit constraints; ambiguity and conflicts (and how you read the logs); performance (flatten deep hierarchies). The interview line: ‘I think in constraints, not frames.’

cards.front: How do you explain SwiftUI’s state trio?
cards.back: @State: view-local value state. @Binding: a reference to someone else’s state (child writes up). @ObservedObject/@StateObject: external reference-type models (StateObject owns the lifetime). The interview line: ‘state flows down, events flow up, ownership is explicit.’

cards.front: How do you explain the SwiftUI layout algorithm?
cards.back: Three steps, parent-driven: the parent proposes a size, the child chooses its size, the parent places it. One pass, no constraint solver — which is why GeometryReader and alignment guides exist for the cases the simple flow can’t express.

cards.front: How do you bridge UIKit and SwiftUI?
cards.back: UIViewRepresentable/UIViewControllerRepresentable to embed UIKit in SwiftUI; UIHostingController to embed SwiftUI in UIKit. The interview line: ‘interop is a migration strategy — wrap the legacy, write new code in SwiftUI.’

quiz.q: Choosing per screen (not per religion) is the senior answer because:
choices: Each framework has real gaps — pragmatism ships, purity stalls
quiz.explain: Interop exists precisely so teams can mix; dogma ignores the gaps.

quiz.q: UIViewRepresentable exists to:
choices: Wrap a UIView so it can live inside a SwiftUI hierarchy
quiz.explain: The representable protocol bridges the imperative UIKit world into declarative SwiftUI.

quiz.q: In SwiftUI layout, the parent:
choices: Asks the child for its size first
Proposes a size; the child decides; the parent places it
quiz.explain: The negotiate-propose-place flow runs in a single pass — fast, but less flexible than Auto Layout.

quiz.q: @Binding exists so that:
choices: A child can read and write a parent’s state without owning it
quiz.explain: Bindings are two-way lenses: the parent owns, the child edits through the lens.

cards.front: GCD in an interview: what do you need cold?
cards.back: Serial vs concurrent queues, QoS classes (user-interactive down to background), async vs sync dispatch, dispatch groups for fan-in, and the iron rule: UI on main, work off main. Deadlock demo: sync onto the current serial queue.

cards.front: OperationQueue vs GCD?
cards.back: OperationQueue: higher-level — dependencies between operations, cancellation, priorities, max concurrency. GCD: lighter, C-level queues. The interview line: ‘dependencies and cancellation buy the Operation abstraction; otherwise GCD.’

cards.front: How do you explain Swift’s structured concurrency?
cards.back: async/await for sequential-looking async code, tasks in hierarchies where children can’t outlive parents, actors for isolated mutable state. The interview line: ‘structure makes lifetimes provable — no more detached callbacks leaking.’

cards.front: What do actors buy you?
cards.back: Isolated mutable state with compiler-enforced exclusive access: only one task touches the actor’s state at a time, and the compiler flags data races at build time. The interview line: ‘actors make the compiler my concurrency reviewer.’

cards.front: Why is main-thread discipline non-negotiable on iOS?
cards.back: UIKit/SwiftUI are not thread-safe: UI updates off the main thread cause undefined behavior — glitches, crashes, corruption. The rule: compute off main (@MainActor for UI-bound code), hop back to main for every UI touch.

quiz.q: @MainActor on a class guarantees:
choices: Its methods run on the main thread — safe for UI work
quiz.explain: The compiler enforces the hop: UI-touching code can’t accidentally run elsewhere.

quiz.q: Swift actors prevent data races by:
choices: Enforcing exclusive, serialized access to their isolated state
quiz.explain: Isolation is checked at compile time: shared mutable state without synchronization can’t compile.

quiz.q: Structured concurrency’s core guarantee is:
choices: Child tasks can’t outlive their parent scope
quiz.explain: The task tree bounds lifetimes: cancellation and completion propagate through the structure.

quiz.q: Operation dependencies give you:
choices: Declarative ordering (‘B after A’) without manual synchronization
quiz.explain: The queue topologically sorts the graph; you declare relationships, not locks.

cards.front: What belongs in UserDefaults — and what doesn’t?
cards.back: Small user preferences (toggles, last-selected tab). NOT secrets (that’s Keychain), NOT large data, NOT anything needing queries or migrations. The interview line: ‘UserDefaults is a preferences plist, not a database.’

cards.front: How do you discuss Codable and file storage?
cards.back: Codable: compiler-synthesized serialization for JSON/plist — custom keys and strategies for real-world APIs. File storage: app sandbox directories (documents vs caches vs tmp) with the right protection. The interview line: ‘Codable for the format, the sandbox for the place.’

cards.front: Core Data stack in 60 seconds?
cards.back: Persistent container → managed object contexts (main for UI, background for work) → persistent store coordinator → SQLite. Faults are lazy loading; the interview traps are threading (one context per queue) and merge policies on conflicts.

cards.front: SwiftData at a glance — how do you position it?
cards.back: Apple’s modern persistence: @Model macro-driven, Swift-native queries with #Predicate, SwiftUI-integrated via @Query — backed by Core Data’s storage. The interview line: ‘SwiftData is the modern API; Core Data knowledge still explains what’s underneath.’

cards.front: Where do secrets go on iOS?
cards.back: Keychain — encrypted, access-controlled (kSecAttrAccessible), surviving app reinstall on the device. The interview line: ‘if it’s a secret, it’s in the Keychain; UserDefaults is a plist anyone can read.’

quiz.q: The choosing rule’s core is:
choices: Access pattern first — queries, relationships, and size decide the store
quiz.explain: Storage choice follows how data is read, written, and related — not habit.

quiz.q: Keychain items vs UserDefaults for a refresh token:
choices: Keychain: encrypted storage with access control; UserDefaults is plaintext-adjacent
quiz.explain: Refresh tokens are long-lived credentials — they get the strongest storage available.

quiz.q: SwiftData’s @Query in SwiftUI provides:
choices: Live-updating fetch results bound to the view — the UI refreshes as data changes
quiz.explain: Declarative data: the view describes what it needs and stays in sync automatically.

quiz.q: Core Data faults are:
choices: Lazily-loaded placeholders — data materializes on first access
quiz.explain: Faulting defers loading until the property is touched — memory-efficient by design.

cards.front: MVC vs MVVM on iOS — the honest comparison?
cards.back: MVC in UIKit decays into Massive View Controller; MVVM extracts state and logic into testable view models with the view as a binding layer. Coordinators own navigation so view controllers stop knowing about each other.

cards.front: Why Hilt (DI) in Android interviews?
cards.back: Constructor injection with generated components: testable (swap fakes), lifecycle-aware scoping, no manual singletons. The interview line: ‘DI inverts control — the class declares needs, Hilt supplies them.’

cards.front: What is unidirectional data flow?
cards.back: State flows down, events flow up: a single source of truth, views render from it, user actions dispatch events that produce new state. Debugging becomes ‘what event produced this state?’ The interview line: ‘one direction, one truth, no mysteries.’

cards.front: How do you layer mobile tests?
cards.back: Unit: view models/logic with fakes — fast, many. UI (XCUITest/Espresso): critical journeys — slow, few. Snapshot: visual regressions on components. The interview line: ‘I test logic in units and reserve devices for what only devices prove.’

cards.front: How do you discuss architecture tradeoffs in an interview?
cards.back: Name the forces (testability, team size, app complexity, longevity), the options with their costs, and your choice with the condition that would change it. The interview line: ‘every architecture is a bet — I state the odds.’

quiz.q: Stating what would change your architecture choice is strong because:
choices: It proves the choice was reasoned from conditions, not dogma
quiz.explain: Conditional choices show engineering judgment; unconditional ones show fashion.

quiz.q: Snapshot tests catch:
choices: Unintended visual changes — pixel-level regressions in components
quiz.explain: Rendered-output comparison: the safety net for UI refactors.

quiz.q: Unidirectional flow’s debugging win is:
choices: State changes have a single traceable path — events in, state out
quiz.explain: Two-way bindings create update cycles; one direction makes every change explainable.

quiz.q: Dependency injection’s testability win is:
choices: Dependencies can be replaced with fakes in tests
quiz.explain: Injected interfaces seam the code: tests substitute fakes without touching production wiring.

cards.front: How do you attack a ‘list-detail with cache’ app spec?
cards.back: Layers: networking (async, cancellable) → repository (network + local cache, single source of truth) → view models (state) → UI. The interview line: ‘the repository is the only class that knows where data lives.’

cards.front: What does a good networking layer look like?

cards.front: How do you turn a guided build into an interview narrative?
cards.back: Problem → constraints → key decisions (with rejected alternatives) → result → what you’d do with more time. The build is proof; the narrative is the delivery vehicle — interviewers probe decisions, so lead with them.

cards.front: The interviewer asks you to go deep on 'App spec: a list-detail app with cache'. What answer structure makes you sound senior?

quiz.q: A build narrative should lead with:
choices: The problem, constraints, and key decisions with alternatives
quiz.explain: Decisions are what get probed; leading with them controls the conversation.

quiz.q: SwiftData’s @Query in SwiftUI provides:
choices: Live-updating fetch results bound to the view — the UI refreshes as data changes
quiz.explain: Declarative data: the view describes what it needs and stays in sync automatically.

quiz.q: Centralizing auth in an interceptor beats per-call headers because:
choices: Token refresh and injection happen once — every call inherits it correctly
quiz.explain: Cross-cutting concerns in one place: no call site can forget the token.

quiz.q: The repository’s job in the list-detail spec is:
choices: Mediating network and cache — one data API for the view models

cards.front: How do you demonstrate Kotlin null-safety depth?
cards.back: Nullable types (?), safe calls (?.), Elvis (?:) for defaults, !! as a justified-only escape hatch, and let/run scoping for non-null blocks. The platform-types warning: Java interop can still hand you null — annotate and defend at boundaries.

cards.front: Data classes vs sealed classes — when each?
cards.back: Data class: value holders with generated equals/hashCode/copy — UI state, DTOs. Sealed class/interface: closed hierarchies for states and results (Loading/Success/Error) with exhaustive when. Together they model UI state safely.

cards.front: What’s the coroutines mental model you’d state?
cards.back: Lightweight sequential-looking async: suspend functions pause without blocking threads, structured concurrency ties child lifetimes to scopes, dispatchers choose the thread pool (Main/IO/Default). ‘Sequential code, asynchronous execution.’

cards.front: Extension functions and scope functions — the interview version?
cards.back: Extensions add behavior without inheritance (nullable receivers included). Scope functions: let (transform nullable), apply (configure), run/with (compute on receiver), also (side effects). The interview line: ‘I pick the scope function by what it returns and what ‘it’ is.’

cards.front: What does Kotlin delegation give you?
cards.back: by lazy: thread-safe lazy init — expensive objects created once on first use. observable/vetoable: react to property changes. Class delegation (by): composition without boilerplate. The interview line: ‘delegation removes the ceremony around common patterns.’

quiz.q: UIViewRepresentable exists to:
choices: Wrap a UIView so it can live inside a SwiftUI hierarchy
quiz.explain: The representable protocol bridges the imperative UIKit world into declarative SwiftUI.

quiz.q: by lazy is preferred over lateinit var when:
choices: The value is immutable and expensive — initialized once, safely, on first access
quiz.explain: lazy gives val semantics with deferred cost; lateinit is a var promise the compiler can’t verify.

quiz.q: let is the right scope function when you want to:
choices: Transform a (possibly null) value and return the result
quiz.explain: let’s lambda returns its last expression — the transform-and-return shape.

quiz.q: A suspend function differs from a blocking call in that it:
choices: Suspends without blocking the underlying thread
quiz.explain: Suspension frees the thread for other coroutines; blocking would pin it.
